```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(gllvmTMB)
```

A species recorded only at one end of an environmental gradient can produce an
extreme fitted slope. A latent loading can also become large when the responses
provide little information about shared variation. The two coefficients play
different roles, so they have separate prior controls. This page shows how to
choose them explicitly and inspect the resulting estimates.

These examples use native TMB Laplace fits with ordinary unit-level latent
effects and complete binary observations. Ordinary `indep()` and Gaussian models also accept the
fixed-effect control. Structured sources, extra grouping tiers, constrained
coefficients, `dep()`, missing responses, non-unit likelihood weights, REML, MSPL,
variational integration and the Julia bridge are outside this initial
support. Eligible ordinary latent models can also request AGHQ; validation of
the combined priors is currently limited to a rank-one probit example. On an
AGHQ fits retain conditional latent modes for loading and ordination point
summaries. Latent-score uncertainty is unavailable, and ordinary profile,
bootstrap and prediction-SE intervals are withheld.
Convergence and the examples below do not establish interval coverage.

# What each prior changes

For response \(j\) at site \(i\), the model is

\[
 y_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{ij}),\qquad
 g(p_{ij})=\alpha_j+\beta_j x_i+\lambda_j z_i,
 \qquad z_i\sim N(0,1).
\]

Here \(g\) is the logit or probit link. The intercept \(\alpha_j\) describes
response \(j\) at the centered predictor value. The slope \(\beta_j\) describes
its association with the measured predictor. The loading \(\lambda_j\)
describes its association with an unmeasured shared site axis. The model
distribution \(z_i\sim N(0,1)\) sets that axis's scale and is present even
when no optional priors are selected.

| Optional control | Coefficients affected | What is pulled toward the prior mean |
|---|---|---|
| `loading_ridge = tau` | Free ordinary between-unit loadings | Shared latent response variation, with mean zero and SD `tau` |
| `fixed_effect_priors` | Named intercepts and slopes | Baseline response levels and measured predictor associations, with a mean and SD for each selected coefficient |

A zero-mean normal prior contributes a quadratic penalty, often called a ridge
penalty. `loading_ridge` adds \(\sum\lambda^2/(2\tau^2)\); the fixed-effect
control adds \(\sum(\beta-m)^2/(2s^2)\), including intercepts when named.
The fixed-effect density also includes its normalizing constant. The loading
penalty omits that constant, so raw objective values from different packages
need this adjustment before comparison.

A loading prior does not directly penalize a separated fixed-effect slope.
The [glmmTMB priors vignette](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/articles/priors.html)
illustrates fixed-effect normal priors for separation. Priors on random-effect
standard deviations, also discussed there, are a further choice; this page's
loading penalty acts directly on the free loading coordinates.

The fitted result is a maximum a posteriori (MAP) point: the mode of the
likelihood times the chosen prior densities. It does not supply posterior
samples. A smaller prior SD increases shrinkage. Choosing an SD is a scientific
assumption to examine through sensitivity fits.
Do not treat the penalized objective, or the likelihood evaluated at its MAP
point, as a maximized likelihood for ordinary AIC or likelihood-ratio tests.

# Choose link-aware scales before fitting

`fixed_effect_priors()` constructs a table from explicit coefficient roles.
It uses the latent-reference normal SD

\[
 s = c\sqrt{v_g+v_{\mathrm{additional}}},\quad
 v_{\mathrm{logit}}=\pi^2/3,\quad v_{\mathrm{probit}}=1.
\]

The multiplier \(c\) can differ for intercepts and slopes. The caller chooses
any additional reference variance before fitting. It is zero by default and
is never estimated from the fitted loadings. In a GLLVM the additional variance
for an item depends on its loadings and other random effects; it is not
automatically one or the number of axes.

This is a scale convention, with no claim of equivalent priors across links or
flat prior probabilities in every model. The helper requires continuous
predictors already centered and scaled to SD 0.5. It does not change the data.
For a binary predictor, declare its zero/one coding and interpret its slope for
that contrast.

[MCMCglmm's source](https://github.com/jarrodhadfield/MCMCglmm/blob/master/R/gelman.prior.R)
and [prior documentation](https://jarrodhadfield.github.io/MCMCglmm/course-notes/glm.html#gelman-prior-sec)
describe related latent-variance references and a transformation back from a
standardized design. That transformation can create correlated intercept and
slope priors. This helper returns independent normals for the supplied
standardized design. It also differs from Gelman's original scaled Cauchy
recommendation. Do not interpret the returned SDs as Cauchy scales.

# Simulate a community on a measured gradient

Three responses share one latent site axis. The continuous predictor has SD
0.5, so the helper's stated convention holds in the actual fitted data.

```{r data}
set.seed(846)
n <- 90
x <- as.numeric(scale(seq(-2, 2, length.out = n))) / 2
z <- rnorm(n)
long <- expand.grid(trait = factor(c("a", "b", "c")), unit = factor(seq_len(n)))
long$x <- rep(x, each = 3)
eta <- rep(c(-0.3, 0.1, 0.4), n) +
  rep(c(0.6, -0.4, 0.3), n) * long$x +
  rep(c(0.5, -0.3, 0.4), n) * rep(z, each = 3)
long$logit_value <- rbinom(nrow(long), 1, plogis(eta))
long$probit_value <- rbinom(nrow(long), 1, pnorm(eta))
sd(x)
```

The logit and probit outcomes are separate simulated datasets. Comparing their
coefficients would mix differences in the link, chosen priors and random draws.

# Worked logit example

The long formula uses `0 + trait`, so its intercept names are `traita`, `traitb`
and `traitc`. They have no conventional `(Intercept)` name. Name the slopes
separately and inspect the actual prior SDs.

`0 + trait` gives each response its own intercept, and `trait:x` gives each its
own slope. The wide formula `traits(a, b, c) ~ 1 + x` expands to these same
response-specific terms. In both calls, `d = 1` selects one shared site axis;
`unique = FALSE` omits an additional independent per-trait site effect, matching
the equation above.

```{r logit-priors}
logit_prior <- fixed_effect_priors(
  "logit", intercepts = paste0("trait", c("a", "b", "c")),
  slopes = paste0("trait", c("a", "b", "c"), ":x"),
  standardized = TRUE, intercept_scale = 2, slope_scale = 1
)
logit_prior
```

These choices give intercept SD about 3.63 and slope SD about 1.81. They are
illustrative reference scales, not tuned values or general recommendations.
Fit the long and wide representations through the same entry point:

```{r logit-fit}
long$value <- long$logit_value
wide <- data.frame(unit = factor(seq_len(n)), x = x,
                   a = long$value[long$trait == "a"],
                   b = long$value[long$trait == "b"],
                   c = long$value[long$trait == "c"])
ctrl <- gllvmTMBcontrol(fixed_effect_priors = logit_prior, loading_ridge = 0.75,
                        svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L)
logit_long <- gllvmTMB(
  value ~ 0 + trait + trait:x + latent(0 + trait | unit, d = 1, unique = FALSE),
  data = long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit", family = binomial("logit"), control = ctrl
)
logit_wide <- gllvmTMB(
  traits(a, b, c) ~ 1 + x + latent(1 | unit, d = 1, unique = FALSE),
  data = wide, unit = "unit", family = binomial("logit"), control = ctrl
)
coef(logit_long)
logit_long$objective_components
```

To see what the priors change, fit a baseline with both optional penalties off,
then fit loading shrinkage alone on exactly the same data.

```{r logit-baseline}
f <- value ~ 0 + trait + trait:x + latent(0 + trait | unit, d = 1, unique = FALSE)
logit_none <- gllvmTMB(f, long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit", family = binomial("logit"),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(loading_ridge = Inf, fixed_effect_priors = NULL,
                            svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L))
logit_loading <- gllvmTMB(f, long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit", family = binomial("logit"),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(loading_ridge = 0.75, svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L))
cbind(no_optional_priors = coef(logit_none), loading_only = coef(logit_loading),
      loading_and_fixed = coef(logit_long))
data.frame(response = c("a", "b", "c"),
  no_optional_priors = abs(as.numeric(logit_none$report$Lambda_B)),
  loading_only = abs(as.numeric(logit_loading$report$Lambda_B)),
  loading_and_fixed = abs(as.numeric(logit_long$report$Lambda_B)))
```

In this seeded example, response b's slope changes from about -1.00 without
the optional priors to -0.99 with the loading prior and -0.93 with both priors.
The absolute-loading table shows the corresponding changes in shared variation;
the sign of a latent axis is arbitrary. Effects
need not all move toward zero: the coefficients are estimated jointly, and a
prior on one component can change another component's estimate.

Ordinary Laplace fitting has no fixed-effect prior by default. Explicitly
selecting `loading_ridge = Inf` also makes the loading choice clear in this
baseline. A loading-only comparison isolates the added fixed-effect prior.

# Worked probit example

Keep the same predictor convention and coefficient roles, but construct new
reference scales for the probit link. Here the intercept SD is 2 and slope SD
is 1. No automatic rescaling of the predictor or the logit estimates occurs.

```{r probit-fit}
probit_prior <- fixed_effect_priors(
  "probit", intercepts = paste0("trait", c("a", "b", "c")),
  slopes = paste0("trait", c("a", "b", "c"), ":x"),
  standardized = TRUE, intercept_scale = 2, slope_scale = 1
)
probit_prior
long$value <- long$probit_value
wide$a <- long$value[long$trait == "a"]
wide$b <- long$value[long$trait == "b"]
wide$c <- long$value[long$trait == "c"]
ctrl <- gllvmTMBcontrol(fixed_effect_priors = probit_prior, loading_ridge = 0.75,
                        svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L)
probit_long <- gllvmTMB(f, long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit",
                       family = binomial("probit"), control = ctrl)
probit_wide <- gllvmTMB(traits(a, b, c) ~ 1 + x + latent(1 | unit, d = 1, unique = FALSE),
                       wide, unit = "unit", family = binomial("probit"), control = ctrl)
probit_none <- gllvmTMB(f, long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit", family = binomial("probit"),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(loading_ridge = Inf, svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L))
cbind(no_optional_priors = coef(probit_none), loading_and_fixed = coef(probit_long))
```

AGHQ is optional for eligible latent models. Check that it ran and converged; an
ineligible request can fall back to Laplace, and a non-converged AGHQ fit
warns that its estimates may be unreliable.

```{r probit-aghq-priors}
aghq_ctrl <- gllvmTMBcontrol(fixed_effect_priors = probit_prior,
  loading_ridge = 0.75, aghq = 5L, aghq_multistart = FALSE,
  svd_start = FALSE, n_init = 1L)
probit_aghq <- gllvmTMB(f, long, trait = "trait", unit = "unit",
  family = binomial("probit"), control = aghq_ctrl)
c(used = probit_aghq$aghq$used, converged = probit_aghq$aghq$converged)
```

The AGHQ local covariance holds the adaptation nodes fixed; its interval
coverage has not been established for these priors.


# Inspect uncertainty and sensitivity

`vcov()` and `sd_report` include the prior precision. They describe local
approximate posterior curvature around the MAP point, conditional on the chosen
scales and model. They do not establish repeated-sampling coverage. Ordinary
interval and prediction-SE helpers refuse these fits while that inference remains
unvalidated. Point predictions remain available.

```{r inspect}
sqrt(diag(vcov(probit_long)))
head(predict(probit_long, type = "response"))
probit_long$fixed_effect_priors
```

Repeat the analysis with scientifically plausible wider and narrower fixed-effect
SDs and loading SDs separately. A direct table can use any finite prior means
and positive SDs for selected coefficients; unnamed coefficients receive no
fixed-effect prior. For an explicitly matched benchmark, SD 10 on all intercepts
and slopes can be paired with loading SD 0.75. That benchmark is not a default
or general advice. Matching two packages also requires matching the data, design,
link, loading constraints, integration and density constants.

```{r direct-table}
benchmark <- data.frame(coefficient = colnames(model.matrix(~ 0 + trait + trait:x, long)),
                         mean = 0, sd = 10)
benchmark
```

For diagnosing separation before fitting, see
[screen binary responses](pre-fit-response-screening.html). The
[rare-species example](rare-species-jsdm.html) covers the separate experimental
MSPL estimator; it cannot be combined with these normal priors.
